topic: The AI Act: which obligations actually bind you, which bind your vendor, and which do not exist until 2027
title: A card belongs to exactly one dimension, so a two-axis obligation-by-actor-by-date table has no representation anywhere in the methodic
expected: A topic whose deliverable is a cross-tab (obligation x actor x applicability date) should be representable as such: a card carrying more than one facet, or a fact record with typed cells, so both axes survive into the board and the script. Note for the judge: this is NOT repairable by a lens as lenses are defined in the SKILL. A lens supplies different COLUMNS; the defect is that a card can only occupy ONE column whatever it is called. Content cannot fix it and a lens cannot fix it — the card-to-dimension cardinality has to change. That is why this is filed `undecided` rather than `lens`.
got: CARD_DIMENSION is `Record<string, DimensionId>` — one card, one column, no second key. The board is a partition, not a matrix. A card reading 'Art. 16 obligations bind providers of high-risk systems from 2 Aug 2026' must choose between `actors` and a date column that does not exist, and destroys whichever axis it does not choose. The only place both axes coexist is inside the free-text `claim` string, which NOTEBOOK-SCHEMA.md:93 argues against ('No prose. Claims are one line') and which no downstream composition step can read structurally.
l2_priority: Attempt to write the obligation table into a real notebook.json and record exactly what is lost. Specifically: can a reviewer recover 'everything that binds a deployer on 2 Aug 2026' from the produced notebook without re-reading the source text? If not, the blocker is confirmed empirically.
refuter_notes: Is this the topic being exotic? No — cross-tabs are ordinary material across the cast's likely space: sanctions (measure x entity x date), streaming rights (title x territory x window), CVE analysis (vuln x version x patch date). Would a competent execution produce it anyway? Only by packing three fields into one claim string, which nothing downstream can read. Is it present somewhere unread? Checked NOTEBOOK-SCHEMA.md, dimensions.ts and conclusions.ts for any multi-tag, facet or matrix affordance — none exists.

title: No pinpoint-citation field and no primary-source precedence rule: an aggregator and the primary instrument are indistinguishable in `facts[].source`
expected: Where a primary instrument exists and is reachable, the methodic should require it and should require a pinpoint (article / recital / section / paragraph), not a document-level gesture. My senior bar is 'article-level citation or it does not exist' — a claim about what the law requires, sourced to a press summary, is the failure mode of my entire field.
got: `facts[].source` is an unconstrained string (the worked notebook contains e.g. '99bitcoins / investingnews price history'). The quality bar asks only that every fact have 'a source, a date and a confidence'. Primacy is handled POST HOC as a Phase 9 confession — 'primary sources you used an aggregator for' — which fires after the notebook is built and imposes no precedence at write time. The worked run demonstrates the tolerated end state: 'Still no PRIMARY on-chain data ... every figure remains aggregator-sourced', recorded as a gap and shipped.
l2_priority: THE decisive L2 check for this creator. Count, in a live run: how many legal claims cite an article number vs a law-firm alert or a press summary where the consolidated text was one search away. L1 can only read the instruction; only L2 shows what the instruction produces.

creator: bill-analysis
topic: The AI Act: which obligations actually bind you, which bind your vendor, and which do not exist until 2027
title: No `authority` field: binding text, recital, annex, implementing act, guidance and commentary all enter as one undifferentiated `facts[]` type
expected: A field recording what legal (or epistemic) weight a source carries, orthogonal to confidence — e.g. authority: binding | interpretive | persuasive | commentary. In my domain an article obliges, a recital explains, a guideline persuades and an alert reports; flattening them is my third pet peeve and the single most common defect in coverage of legislation.
got: One record type: `{id, claim, load_bearing, source, confidence, as_of, note?}`. `confidence` is orthogonal and cannot substitute — a recital is CERTAINLY text and CERTAINLY not binding, so grading it `high` says the opposite of the true thing. The one worked heuristic in the schema, 'Vendor research is low by default', has no analogue for 'commentary is low where the primary text was available'. `note?` is free text and, by the schema's own principle ('does a step of the composition procedure read this?'), is consumed by nothing.
l2_priority: In a live run, check whether any recital or guideline is stated in the script with the grammar of an obligation ('the Act requires'). One instance promotes this to a safety finding.

title: `as_of` is a currency date, not an applicability date — a staged-commencement topic has nowhere to record 'applies from', and using `as_of` corrupts the currency model
expected: A distinct `applies_from` / effective-date field for topics where a claim's date is a property of the world rather than of the research. Entry into force vs entry into application is my second pet peeve and it is the difference between a correct video and a costly one.
got: The only date on a fact is `as_of` — 'every fact is dated. This drives `currency`' — i.e. a freshness stamp. The AI Act's staged commencement (1 Aug 2024 in force; 2 Feb 2025 prohibitions; 2 Aug 2025 GPAI; 2 Aug 2026 general; 2 Aug 2027 Art. 6(1)) has no home. Worse than absent: writing 2 Aug 2027 into `as_of` feeds a future date into `currency.expires_first` / `durable[]`, so the honesty mechanism silently mis-computes. The one date field offered means the opposite of the date the topic needs.
l2_priority: Write the commencement dates into a real notebook and observe where they land and what `currency` then reports. Confirm whether the corruption is real or whether a researcher naturally routes around it.

creator: bill-analysis
topic: The AI Act: which obligations actually bind you, which bind your vendor, and which do not exist until 2027
title: Nothing prevents a conclusion from stating a normative requirement — an unsourced model inference can be phrased as a statement of what the law obliges
expected: A modality constraint: in regulated domains a conclusion may state a CONSEQUENCE of a reading ('most firms will discover this too late') but never a REQUIREMENT ('deployers who rebrand a system inherit provider obligations'). The second is a legal claim, reasoned rather than researched, sitting in a column whose own header says it has no sources.
got: No such rule exists. `useFor` ('thesis'|'reversal'|'reframe'|'steel-man'|'colour') governs PLACEMENT, not modality. The safeguards are opt-in gating plus a mandatory falsifier, and a normative claim satisfies both — it can carry a perfectly good falsifier ('wrong if Commission guidance says otherwise') and still be a statement of law. The gating risk runs backwards: a fluent, plausible, wrong sentence about what the Act requires is exactly the kind a reviewer gates IN, because it reads as insight. Exposure bar: viewers make compliance decisions from these videos.
l2_priority: Generate conclusions on this topic and count how many are phrased normatively. This is the exposure-class finding the rubric says only L2 produces; L1 can only show the constraint is missing, not that it bites.

creator: bill-analysis
topic: The AI Act: which obligations actually bind you, which bind your vendor, and which do not exist until 2027
title: The `unhinged` tier is DEFINED as a motive claim while the falsifier rule requires checkability, and the skill rules motive falsifiers uncheckable
expected: Either the tier is defined by heat rather than by claim-class, or the falsifier standard for it is stated explicitly — e.g. 'a motive conclusion must be falsifiable by observable BEHAVIOUR, not by intent.' As written the tier's definition and its own mandatory rule contradict each other.
got: LEAP_NOTE.unhinged: 'A claim about MOTIVE, which is the least verifiable kind of claim there is — nobody can source what someone intended.' `falsifiableBy` is REQUIRED. SKILL.md rules that "wrong if their intent was different" is not checkable and 'an uncheckable falsifier is a fig leaf'. PARTIAL REFUTATION, recorded honestly: the one worked instance evades the contradiction — c-reserve-was-the-product makes a motive claim about a named administration and falsifies it on BEHAVIOUR ('a funded, audited reserve with a published coin count'), which is genuinely checkable. So the falsifier requirement did constrain it in practice. The good move exists and is undocumented; the definition still invites the bad one. On my topic the bad one is 'the Commission never intended the GPAI tier to bind US labs' — legislative-intent speculation with no checkable falsifier.
l2_priority: Generate an `unhinged` conclusion on a legislative topic and score its falsifier for checkability. If it falsifies on behaviour, the rule holds and this is refuted — a documentation finding at most. If it falsifies on intent, it is confirmed and the tier needs a stated standard.

title: Engine selection has no exposure input, and the schema actively instructs the researcher to exclude it
expected: Each engine should carry a note on what a wrong render COSTS, and `engine_fit` should be permitted — ideally required — to weigh it. Engine D is the highest-exposure engine in the catalogue by construction: its output is a verdict, and a verdict rendered over a contested reading of a statute is a legal opinion with a hook, delivered to compliance officers by someone who is not their counsel.
got: ENGINES.md discriminates on exactly one variable, 'the viewer's pleasure', and the choosing table is purely shape-based; there is no consequence or exposure note against any engine. D is recommended precisely where 'the honest answer is contested'. NOTEBOOK-SCHEMA.md then instructs that engine_fit is 'assessed against knowledge/ENGINES.md from the *material*, not from taste' — so a researcher following the instruction faithfully EXCLUDES risk, because risk is not material. Symptom: 6 of 7 engines plausibly fit my notebook (a smell per the SKILL), because narrative shape is not the binding constraint on my topic and the catalogue has no axis for the constraint that is.
l2_priority: Render this notebook through Engine D and have the creator state what their lawyer would say about the verdict section. This is the L2 exposure review and I expect it to be the sharpest artifact of the run.
